(B) A cultural program through which China adopted Korean technology
(C) A defensive alliance against Silla raids on China's frontier
(D) Acknowledged Chinese superiority in exchange for trade and security
explanation: Silla's tribute missions to Chang'an were the price of admission to the Chinese world order: by ritually acknowledging Chinese superiority, Silla secured access to Chinese markets, luxury goods, and diplomatic backing while running its own affairs — a mutually useful fiction of hierarchy. (A) is wrong because China withdrew its forces from Korea as part of the arrangement; no occupation sustained it. (B) is wrong because silk and porcelain technology flowed from China outward, not the reverse. (C) is wrong because Silla was the peninsular power seeking Chinese favor, not a raider of China's northern frontier.

stem: As shogunal authority decayed in fifteenth-century Japan, lesser vassals seized power from their own superiors. This pattern is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) Gekokujo, the overthrow of superiors by their own vassals
(B) The granting of political equality to women
(C) The restoration of the emperor as central political figure
(D) The rise of sustained Sino-Japanese military antagonism
explanation: As Ashikaga shogunal authority decayed in the fifteenth century, lesser vassals and provincial deputies overthrew their own superiors and seized their domains — the age of gekokujo, 'the low overthrowing the high.' This produced the Sengoku daimyo, warlords who consolidated taxation and public works within their own territories. (B) is wrong because women lost, not gained, political standing in this era. (C) is wrong because the emperor remained a figurehead while real power devolved downward. (D) is wrong because Sino-Japanese relations were not defined by antagonism in this period.

stem: Which Song policy best explains why the dynasty remained vulnerable to northern nomadic powers despite its wealth?
options: (A) Peasant protests against land reform caused empire-wide famine
(B) The Delhi Sultanate blockaded the Silk Roads with its armies, cutting off all Song trade with the west
(C) The dynasty privileged civil officials over the military and bought peace with tribute payments
(D) Widespread opium use caused social and economic collapse
explanation: Song emperors elevated civil scholar-officials and distrusted the military, funding defense poorly and paying tribute to the Khitan Liao and later the Jurchen Jin to buy peace. That policy kept the dynasty culturally brilliant but militarily soft, so northern nomadic powers could eventually overwhelm it. (A) is wrong because famine-as-protest does not explain the Song's military collapse. (B) is wrong because the Delhi Sultanate, far to the southwest, did not blockade Song trade routes. (D) is wrong because the opium crisis belongs to the nineteenth century, not the Song.

stem: A stone frieze from Gandhara (in modern Pakistan) shows the Buddha carved with flowing Greek-style robes and a naturalistic stance borrowed from Hellenistic sculpture. What does this best illustrate about Hellenistic cultural exchange?
stimulus: The frieze, carved in the centuries after Alexander's conquests, depicts the Buddha with deeply folded Greco-Roman drapery, a naturalistic body stance, and wavy hair tied in a Greco-style topknot — yet the subject is unmistakably the Buddha, seated among Indian devotees.
options: (A) The Greeks imposed their religion on India
(B) Indians had no artistic traditions before the Greeks arrived
(C) Alexander banned all local art forms
(D) Conquered peoples adapted Greek artistic forms to their own religious purposes
explanation: The Buddha wears Greek drapery and stands in a Greek pose, but the figure is the Buddha, serving a Buddhist devotional purpose. Greek forms were borrowed, yet local artisans and patrons decided what those forms would mean — conquest supplied a visual vocabulary, but the conquered wrote the sentences. (A) is wrong because the image shows a Buddhist figure, not a Greek god imposed on India. (B) is wrong because India had rich artistic traditions long before Alexander. (C) is wrong because the frieze itself proves local art flourished under Hellenistic influence.

stem: After Alexander's death, his generals founded kingdoms in Egypt and Persia that lasted for centuries. What made these kingdoms 'Hellenistic' rather than simply Greek?
options: (A) They used only the Greek language
(B) They systematically erased all native customs
(C) They blended Greek institutions with local administrative and cultural traditions
(D) They governed as democracies on the Athenian model
explanation: The Ptolemies in Egypt and Seleucids in Persia kept pharaonic rituals, Babylonian temples, and local bureaucracies running while adding Greek cities, gymnasia, and administration on top. 'Hellenistic' names that fusion — Greek-style monarchy ruling through adapted native institutions. (A) is wrong because these kingdoms operated in Egyptian, Aramaic, and Persian as well as Greek. (B) is wrong because they preserved and patronized local customs rather than erasing them. (D) is wrong because they were monarchies, not Athenian-style democracies.

stem: Alexander adopted Persian court rituals, married Persian noblewomen, and recruited Persians into his army. How did his Macedonian veterans react?
options: (A) They celebrated the policies enthusiastically and adopted Persian dress themselves
(B) They converted to Zoroastrianism
(C) They mutinied, seeing Persian practices as a betrayal of Macedonian identity
(D) They had no recorded opinion on the matter
explanation: Macedonian veterans mutinied at Opis in 324 BCE, protesting Persian dress, Persian marriages, and Persian troops in the army — they saw their king going native. The episode shows that cultural fusion imposed from the throne had sharp limits when it collided with the conquerors' own identity. (A) is wrong because the veterans protested and in some cases mutinied. (B) is wrong because there is no evidence of mass Macedonian conversion to Zoroastrianism. (D) is wrong because the sources record loud, organized resentment.

stem: The Mongols exempted religious clergy of all faiths from taxes and forced labor. What best explains this policy?
stimulus: At the height of their power, the Mongol khans ruled a vast domain where peoples who had once been enemies lived side by side in relative peace, and nearly every religion was tolerated. The legal code first issued under Chinggis Khan regulated relations among these peoples and opened a new era of international contact. From Eastern Europe to southern China, merchants and travelers could cross the well-guarded Mongol territories without fearing for their lives or goods. The great belt of Mongol land, covering or linking most of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, served as a bridge between the civilizations of the Eastern Hemisphere. Caravans and embassies crossing Mongol lands carried new foods, inventions, and ideas from one civilized region to another, and from settled societies to the nomads who acted as go-betweens. Safe roads enriched merchants and built wealthy, cosmopolitan cities, while the movement of crops and technologies became a powerful engine of economic and social development.
options: (A) Chinggis Khan personally converted to each major religion
(B) The Mongols despised all religion and wanted clergy fully dependent on the khan's favor
(C) The Quran required the Mongols to tolerate other faiths
(D) Exempting clergy won the loyalty of influential religious leaders across the empire
explanation: The Mongols were a tiny ruling minority over a vast empire of Muslims, Buddhists, Christians, and others. Exempting clergy from taxes and labor bought the goodwill — or at least the neutrality — of the religious leaders who shaped popular opinion, a cheap price for stability. It was strategy, not conviction. (A) is wrong because Chinggis Khan followed Mongol shamanism and never converted. (B) is wrong because the Mongols patronized religions rather than despising them. (C) is wrong because Mongol policy had nothing to do with Quranic requirements.

(B) To move official messages and intelligence rapidly across vast distances

(D) To transport tribute grain to the capital

For a nomadic dynasty ruling sedentary millions, fast information was the nervous system of control. (A) is wrong because the yam served officials and the military, not casual travelers. stem: How did the Mongol period shape the rise of Moscow among the Russian principalities?

options: (A) Moscow's princes grew rich and powerful as the khans' tribute-collectors
(B) The Mongols made Moscow their imperial capital
(C) Moscow led the resistance that expelled the Mongols in 1240
(D) The Mongols converted Moscow to Islam
explanation: The khans appointed Moscow's princes as their chief tribute-collectors, letting them skim wealth and crush rival principalities with Mongol backing. options: (A) Both relied on native elites and local traditions to keep order and collect tribute

stem: The hymn says the Brahman came from Purusa's mouth and the Shudra from his feet. What social claim does this body imagery make?
stimulus: Paraphrase of the Purusa hymn from the Rig-Veda (c. 1500-1000 BCE), India's oldest surviving literature: Purusa is the lord of the immortals, sustained by ritual offerings. When the gods sacrificed Purusa as their offering — spring as the clarified butter, summer as the kindling, autumn as the oblation — the sacrifice itself became the source of all things. From that fully offered sacrifice were born the sacred hymns and chants, the sacrificial formulas, the horses, and the cattle, goats, and sheep. Then the gods divided Purusa: his mouth became the Brahman (priest), his arms the Rajanya (warrior-ruler), his thighs the Vaishya (producer-trader), and from his feet the Shudra (servant) was born. So were the worlds fashioned — the gods sacrificing the sacrifice with the sacrifice, in the first of all rites.
options: (A) All social ranks are spiritually equal
(B) The body-part mapping is random and meaningless
(C) Social hierarchy is divinely built into the structure of creation
(D) The hymn is a medical description of human anatomy and bodily functions
explanation: Mapping the Brahman to the mouth, the Kshatriya to the arms, the Vaishya to the thighs, and the Shudra to the feet presents rank as anatomy — built into the cosmic body at creation. Hierarchy is thereby not a human convention but the structure of the universe itself. (A) is wrong because the hymn ranks the varnas explicitly; it does not teach equality. (B) is wrong because the body parts are deliberately hierarchical, from mouth down to feet. (D) is wrong because the hymn is a cosmogonic religious text, not a medical one.

stem: The Purusa hymn dates to roughly 1500-1000 BCE, among the oldest Hindu scriptures. What does its account of the varnas' origins demonstrate?

options: (A) Caste had no religious basis in early Hinduism and arose purely from politics
(B) The British invented the caste system
(C) Caste was embedded with divine authority in Hinduism's oldest scriptures
(D) The hymn argues against the varna order
explanation: The hymn belongs to the Rig-Veda, composed around 1500-1000 BCE — the fountainhead of Hindu scripture. That the varna order appears in India's oldest religious text shows caste was sacralized from the very beginning, carrying divine authority rather than being a late or purely secular invention. (A) is wrong because the hymn itself gives caste a religious origin. (B) is wrong because British colonialism came three millennia later. (D) is wrong because the hymn affirms the varna order; it does not oppose it.

stem: The medieval bhakti movement taught that devotion to god outranked birth, and its revered saints included low-caste poets. What does this show about caste in practice?

options: (A) The caste system disappeared in medieval India, replaced by an egalitarian order
(B) Bhakti devotion reinforced Brahman authority
(C) Religious movements could challenge caste rigidity from within Hindu tradition
(D) No one in Indian history ever questioned caste
explanation: Bhakti saints like Kabir and Ravidas — themselves of low or humble birth — taught that loving devotion to god mattered more than ritual purity or birth, drawing followers across caste lines. That caste could be challenged from inside Hindu tradition shows the system was contested in practice, not monolithic. (A) is wrong because caste ideology and hierarchy persisted for centuries after. (B) is wrong because bhakti devotion often bypassed Brahman ritual authority rather than reinforcing it. (D) is wrong because the bhakti critics themselves prove questioning happened.

stem: Before 1492, the Americas were isolated from Afro-Eurasian trade networks. What was the fundamental reason?
options: (A) American peoples banned all foreign trade
(B) The Americas had no goods worth trading
(C) Oceans too wide for existing ships physically isolated the Americas
(D) Europeans deliberately hid the Americas from Asian merchants to monopolize trade
explanation: The Atlantic is roughly 3,000 miles wide and the Pacific far wider; no ship of the ancient or medieval world could carry enough water and provisions to cross them. Afro-Eurasian networks stopped at the water's edge because the technology to cross did not yet exist.

stem: The Upanishads shift focus from external sacrifice to inner realization of Brahman. What religious change does this represent?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a passage from the Upanishads (c. 1000 BCE): He contains all works and desires, all perfumes and all tastes. He enfolds the entire universe, and in silence loves all. This is the Spirit within my heart; this is Brahman. To him I shall go when I pass beyond this life, as will all who have faith and do not doubt.
options: (A) A shift from ritual sacrifice to inner knowledge as the path to liberation
(B) The rejection of all gods
(C) The invention of the caste system
(D) The adoption of Buddhist teachings on the Four Noble Truths centuries before the Buddha
explanation: Early Vedic religion centered on elaborate sacrifices performed by priests to win divine favor. The Upanishads turn inward: liberation comes from realizing one's identity with Brahman through knowledge and meditation, not from ritual correctness. It was a philosophical revolution within the tradition.

stem: The speaker hopes to 'come to Brahman' after death. How does this Hindu goal differ from the Buddhist goal of nirvana?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a passage from the Upanishads (c. 1000 BCE): He contains all works and desires, all perfumes and all tastes. He enfolds the entire universe, and in silence loves all. This is the Spirit within my heart; this is Brahman. To him I shall go when I pass beyond this life, as will all who have faith and do not doubt.
options: (A) They are identical goals
(B) Buddhism has no concept of liberation and teaches only obedience to priests
(C) Hinduism denies any afterlife
(D) Hinduism seeks union with Brahman; Buddhism seeks extinction of self
explanation: Moksha is release into union with Brahman, the ultimate reality; nirvana is the extinguishing of the self and its cravings. Both seek escape from rebirth, but Hinduism's goal affirms a universal Self while Buddhism denies a permanent self exists.

stem: The Upanishads are part of the Vedas, Hinduism's oldest scriptures, yet their content is philosophical rather than ritual. What does this show about Hinduism?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a passage from the Upanishads (c. 1000 BCE): He contains all works and desires, all perfumes and all tastes. He enfolds the entire universe, and in silence loves all. This is the Spirit within my heart; this is Brahman. To him I shall go when I pass beyond this life, as will all who have faith and do not doubt.
options: (A) Hinduism contains both ritual and philosophical strands within one tradition
(B) Hinduism consists only of ritual sacrifice, with no philosophical tradition whatsoever
(C) The Upanishads are Buddhist texts
(D) Hinduism has no scriptures
explanation: The Vedas contain hymns for sacrifice and the Brahmanas' ritual manuals, but also the Upanishads' philosophy and later the epics' stories. Hinduism holds these together as one unfolding tradition rather than splitting into separate religions.

stem: The Andes had the domesticated llama, yet no plow agriculture or wheeled transport developed. Why didn't llamas play the role of Eurasian oxen?
stimulus: The 1616 illustration by Guaman Poma de Ayala shows several Andean farmers working a field with a wooden foot plow, pressing it into the earth with their feet while others follow behind.
options: (A) Llamas are too small and weak to pull plows or heavy carts
(B) Andean farmers were too lazy to use animals, preferring to carry burdens themselves
(C) Llamas were sacred and could not be worked
(D) Andeans did not know the wheel existed
explanation: Llamas stand barely four feet tall and can carry only about a hundred pounds; they cannot pull a plow or a loaded cart. The Andes simply had no animal capable of doing an ox's work, so the plow and the cart could never pay off no matter who knew the principle.
